name: Interlingue (Occidental)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Wikipedia, 'Interlingue', Stress section (citing the Occidental standard grammar; read 2026-08-31)
earlier_scan.note: Fixed rule: stress the vowel before the final consonant; certain endings stress-neutral; irregular stress marked with acute accent.

new_statements.quote: 1. Li accentu tonic es situat ordinarmen sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant. [...] 2. Li finales -bil, -ic, (si it es pronunciat [ik]), -im, -ul es ínaccentuat e attrae li accentu al precendent syllabe, mem si li precedent syllabe es un de ti quar syllabes (finales atonic): labil, nobil, possibil, stabil; archaic, [...] 3. Li finale -s del plurale e li finales -men e -um es ínaccentuat e ne have influentie al accentu del céteri parol-parte (finales enclitic): doctor, doctores; linea, lineas; [...] 4. Paroles ne havent vocales ante li ultim consonant es accentuat sur li unesim vocale: die, deo, noi, tui [...] 6. In li casus ne conform al regules supra-citat, li accentu es scrit (accentu graphic): bontá, mamá, qualitá; allé, bebé, café
new_statements.translation: 1. The tonic accent is ordinarily placed on the vowel before the last consonant. [...] 2. The finals -bil, -ic (if pronounced [ik]), -im, -ul are unaccented and draw the accent onto the preceding syllable, even if the preceding syllable is one of these four syllables (atonic finals): labil, nobil, possibil, stabil; archaic, [...] 3. The plural final -s and the finals -men and -um are unaccented and have no influence on the accent of the rest of the word (enclitic finals): doctor, doctores; linea, lineas; [...] 4. Words having no vowel before the last consonant are accented on the first vowel: die, deo, noi, tui [...] 6. In cases not conforming to the rules cited above, the accent is written (graphic accent): bontá, mamá, qualitá; allé, bebé, café
new_statements.citation: Janotta, K. (compiler; with E. Pigal, A. Deminger, E. de Wahl). 1929. Complet Grammatica de Occidental. I-esim Capitul: Phonologie, C. Accentuation. Cosmoglotta (Mauer bei Wien: Occidental-Union), Annu VIII, Nr 65 (10), Octobre 1929, pp. 165-166.
new_statements.locator: p. 165, C. Accentuation, articles 1-3 (PDF page 3); articles 4-6 on p. 166 (PDF page 4)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: stress the vowel immediately preceding the word's last consonant, i.e. the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant (doctOr, generAl) and the syllable before a final vowel or vowel sequence otherwise (farIne, famIlie, AustrIa; postvocalic iV/uV sequences do not count as separate syllables). Stress-neutral material: the atonic finals -bil, -ic, -im, -ul push stress to the preceding syllable (possIbil, herOic, Ultim, artIcul), and plural -s, adverbial -men and -um are ignored (doctOres, rapIdmen, mAximum). Words with no vowel before the last consonant stress the first vowel (dIe, dEo). All lexical deviations are marked orthographically with an acute (bontá, café, númere, límite). Prescriptive rule of a planned language; Haas 1956 par. 8 restates it identically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Art. 3: -men, being shortened Latin 'mente', may receive a secondary accent (respectabilmen, sobrimen). Art. 5 (p.166): in compounds each part may bear a tonic accent; if the first (determining) part is a noun, adjective or the negative prefix ín- it takes the primary accent and the second part a secondary one; if the first part is a particle it takes no accent or a secondary accent and the second part takes the primary (férrovía, ínpracticábil vs. rétrovenír, áttraér). Haas 1956 par. 8: in compounds and prefixed words the principal part follows the rules, the others may receive a secondary accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Atonic finals -bil, -ic, -im, -ul; enclitic finals -s (plural), -men, -um; vowel-final monosyllabic-type words die, deo, noi, tui, boa (first vowel); irregular words marked with written accent, e.g. bontá, café, depó, menú, heróe, númere, límite, spíritu, and contrary to art. 2-3 amíc, formíca, ínterim, parfúm; written accent may be omitted on very frequent words (amic, femina, inter) except on final vowels (Haas par. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation/orthographic forms of a constructed (planned) language; the statement is prescriptive (normative grammar published by the Occidental-Union), not a description of recorded speech. Language renamed Interlingue in 1949 without change to the rule (Haas 1956 gives the same rule).
new_statements.identity_note: Occidental (name used 1922-1949) and Interlingue (name since 1949) are the same planned language, ISO 639-3 [ile], Glottolog inte1260; Haas 1956 states the rename did not change the language. Not to be confused with Interlingua (IALA 1951, ISO [ina]), a different constructed language. The rule quoted is a normative rule of a constructed language, not a fieldwork description.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en), 'Interlingue', section Phonology > Stress (wikitext fetched sources 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Second-hand: same wording as MacLeod 2019; footnotes cite Cosmoglotta A 1929 p.165 (ANNO scan) and Haas 1956 (pbworks English translation). Used only to identify the primary sources.

sources.citation: Haas, F. 1956. Grammatica de Interlingue in English (English translation; HTML adaptation by Sebastian Hartwig 2009, interlingue.pbworks.com, Wayback 2013). Section STRESS, par. 8.
sources.note: 'The primary stress is on the vowel before the last consonant, but not on the four syllables bil, ic, im, ul, which take the accent on the preceding syllable, even if this is bil, ic, im, ul. A simple s and the two syllables men and um at the end of the word do not change the stress of the preceding part of the word. If those rules are not applicable, one stresses the first vowel of the word.'

sources.citation: Haas, Fritz. 1956. Grammatica de Interlingue in Interlingue. Winterthur (Svissia): Interlingue-Servicie. (Digitalisat de S. Belitzky; web copy at panix.com/~bartlett/ via Wayback 2021-02-11.) Section ACCENTUATION, par. 8-9.
sources.note: Par. 8: 'Li accentu primari sta sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant, ma ne sur li quar síllabes bil, ic, im, ul, queles porta li accentu al precedent síllab, mem si ti-ci es bil, ic, im, ul. Un simplic s e li du síllabes men e um in li fine del parol ne changea li accentuation del precedent parol-parte. Si ti regules ne es aplicabil, on accentua li prim vocal del parol.' Irregular stress marked with written accent (é preferred); in compounds the principal part follows the rules, other parts may get secondary accent. Same rule as Janotta 1929.

sources.citation: Ramstedt, A. Z. 1929. Occidental Course in 10 Lessons (orig. German, Occidental-Buro Berlin); English translation, orthographic modernization and new additions by David MacLeod (2019). occidental-lang.com PDF, 92 pp. Section 0 'Pronunciation and accent' > Stress, PDF p. 2; note on -men PDF p. 81.
sources.note: 'Words are generally stressed on the vowel before the final consonant: intercalar, parol, forme. Pluralizing a noun does not change the stress... The endings -bil, -ic, -im, -ul and -um do not change the stress... nor does the adverbial ending -men...' plus diphthong, die/deo, compound and written-accent clauses. This paragraph (a 2019 translator addition) is verbatim the text of the Wikipedia Stress section that the earlier scan quoted.
